L. General Description of the Surrounding Neighborhoods and Population and Growth Characteristics 1,2
Planning Agencies can seldom limit their concern to the population within a single geographic boundary. In most instances, it is important for an agency to study both a broader area which includes its own format jurisdiction, and also smaller subdivisions of its jurisdiction.
In the context of population studies, this requires subdivision of the areas of jurisdiction into planning districts or analysis zones and consideration of the present and future population in each of these subareas. In a large urban area the three levels of geographic distinctions are 1) metropolitan area, 2) city or village, and 3) district.
Analysis and projection of migration to or from the "Metro area" will be largely related to studies of judgements about the economic base and employment of the metro area. For projecting metro area migration the data required include the numbers in each sex, race and age group of those moving from one area to another, for all pairs of areas. Such data are available only for some large regions and for the nation as a whole, generally from sample surveys.
Past migration may give some clues about future migration. However, planners' assumptions about future metro area migrations will no doubt continue to be based chiefly on judgements about the migration implications of economic projections and plans. It is at this point that the major interaction between planners' economic studies and population studies must occur.
